“Sufficient Growth”
53A-1-1107.5
 (2) (a) For the purpose of determining whether a student demonstrates sufficient growth in
the 2014-15 school year, or a succeeding school year, in language arts, mathematics, or
science as provided in Section 53A-1-1107, the board shall establish a year 2 growth target
for a student for each statewide assessment the student takes.
 (b) A student demonstrates sufficient growth if the student's scale score on a
statewide assessment in year 2 is equal to or exceeds the year 2 growth target established
pursuant to Subsections (2)(c) and (2)(d).
 (c) The board shall establish a year 2 growth target for each cohort of students with
the same scale score on a particular statewide assessment in year 1.
 (d) (i) The board shall establish a year 2 growth target based on actual student growth
in the 2014-15 school year as measured by statewide assessments administered at the end of
the 2013-14 and 2014-15 school years.
 (ii) Among a cohort of students with the same scale score on a particular statewide
assessment in the 2013-14 school year, the scale score of the student who scores on a
similar statewide assessment in the 2014-15 school year, at a percentile determined by the
board in rule, becomes the year 2 growth target for statewide assessments administered in
the 2014-15 school year and succeeding years for any student with a year 1 scale score that
is the same as the cohort's scale score in the 2013-14 school year.

Options Discussed by TAC, PAC, and State Board
 1. Tie the target a student growth percentile (SGP) of 30
 2. Set the next-year target scale score to be the cut score one level up from
 the current-year performance level (or the cut score for the highest
 performance level for students already achieving at this level)
 3. Set next-year target scale scores separately for each current-year scale
 score deciles by calculating the average gain score for that decile based
 on prior years’ data, and adding that to the current-year scale score for
 every student.
 4. Set the next-year target scale score to the Adequate Growth Percentile
 (AGP) necessary to move to the next performance level over a specified
 number of years or remain in the top performance level for a specified
 number of years
 5. Set sufficient growth to an SGP of 40 for each student

 UT Technical Advisory Committee_Jan. 13-14, 2016 3

Preferred Option: SGP = 40
 • Set the target at the 40th growth percentile for each
 student
 • Determine the percentage of students in each school
 meeting the growth target
 • Follow the Grading Schools aggregation rules

But…
• Utah’s key legislative leaders insisted that the law
 requires the use of a specific scale score instead of
 framing the target in the SGP metric

• This is not unique to Utah. Previously, Arizona and
 Indiana have requested conversion of an SGP target to a
 scale score target.
• The software used to calculates SGPs (SGP package) was
 extended several years ago to support that use case.

 UT Technical Advisory Committee_Jan. 13-14, 2016 5

• Unfortunately, there are many misconceptions regarding
 SGP/scale score targets

• On the following slides, we present some key properties
 associated with such targets and then offer two options
 for fulfilling the legislative request

 UT Technical Advisory Committee_Jan. 13-14, 2016 6

Zero-sum game
 • A 40th percentile SGP/scale score target does not result
 in a zero-sum game where 40 percent of students “lose”
 and 60 percent of the students “win”
 • Targets are set a year in advance so (ideally) teachers
 know each student’s scale score goal at the beginning of
 the school year.
 • If the system improves in the ensuing year, then a higher
 percentage of students will reach their target than in the
 base year.
 – That is, more than 60% of students (even, in theory, 100% of
 students) can meet or exceed their target.

 UT Technical Advisory Committee_Jan. 13-14, 2016 7

Comparable Targets
• Basing targets on SGP=40 ensures that all student have
 the same relative difficulty in reaching their target, even
 though scale score increases/gains differ by student
• There is a misconception that scale score increases/gain
 scores are uniform regardless of where a student starts
 – This simply is not true!

• Establishing a single SGP target of 40 creates a uniform
 level of difficulty for all students even though the scale
 score changes for each student will differ

Two Approaches
• Single Prior
• Multiple Priors

• Student growth projections, which are the basis of the
 SGP/scale score targets utilized by Utah and other states
 can be calculated using either a single or multiple scale
 score priors (if available).
• The use of single or multiple scale score priors is usually
 done to be consistent with the way in which SGPs are
 calculated.

 UT Technical Advisory Committee_Jan. 13-14, 2016 23

Single Prior
 • Ensures that every student with the same prior (Year 1)
 score will have the same scale score target (Year 2)
 • An advantage for using a single prior stems from the
 belief that it is more straightforward to communicate a
 target based upon a single rather than multiple priors
 • Disadvantage is that the single prior is the least accurate
 (and perhaps least reliable) case of SGPs

 UT Technical Advisory Committee_Jan. 13-14, 2016 24

Multiple Priors
 • SGPs are almost always calculated with multiple scale
 score priors (when available). Thus, projections for
 students also utilize the same multiple scale score priors.
 • Multiple priors lead to more accurate individual targets.
 The disadvantage to using multiple priors often stems
 from the belief that it is more difficult to communicate a
 target based upon multiple priors than a single prior
 – For example, two students with the same immediately
 prior score may (likely will) have different targets
 based on the full score history

Single versus multiple prior based targets

 • Low ELA achieving student
 in 2014 (below prof/360)
 who had high growth in
 2015 (SGP=92) raising their
 status (proficient/450).
 • Top Figure: Using only 2015
 Score to set target for 2016
 gives a scale score target of
 465 (SGP 40 with 1 prior).
 • Bottom Figure: Using both
 2014 and 2015 Scores to set
 student target for 2016
 gives a scale score target of
 445 (SGP 40 with 2 priors) .
 • Ignoring the 2014 scale
 score sets too high a target
 for the student.

Single versus multiple prior based targets

 • High ELA achieving student

 • Top Figure: Using only 2015
 Score to set target for 2016

 • Ignoring the 2014 scale

Discussion and Recommendations

 • Which option seems most promising and why?
 • Does the TAC think the increased accuracy associated
 with using multiple priors is worth the potential
 explanatory challenges?
 • If so, can the TAC suggest some good strategies for
